cs.t: Amazing to see it still getting sold now in 2023. I own two of these and while they now sit in my garage I've probably used them for 15 years. I bought them exactly for the reason laid out in the article - this router has solid hardware and the fact you could out just openwrt/ddwrt on it was amazing.
cs.th: The WRT54GL: A 54Mbps router from 2005 still makes millions for Linksys (2016)

cs.t: As a developer I haven't hit the point where I can have too many cores.  When I can run three or six VMs (linux server), each allocated 2 cores (hyperthreaded ones are ok) and at least 1GB RAM each, while simultaneously abusing my browser with too many tabs, with cycles to spare for big desktop apps (Gimp, LibreOffice, etc), then I won't care so much about cores anymore. That's possible on high-end machines, but I'm looking forward to mid-level laptops being able to do that too. I do agree that a lot of performance will come from better coding, though.  I can see that in my Linksys WRT54GL router, which is 2004 hardware that runs better than most everything else available today, thanks in large part to 8 years of open source software evolution in the firmware. When software has time to evolve and mature on stable hardware, it's really cool to see the performance that can be weened out of even old hardware.

cs.t: Had an army of these things doing bridge wifi all over my house for many years, well past their use buy date. I still have them in a box, too slow to be of much use now. I still have the reputation with tech friends as "The WRT guy". These days I buy GL.iNet routers and run OpenWrt.
